stem: A 26-year-old woman has felt nervous and shaky and lost 5 kg in the 6 weeks since giving birth. Pulse is 104/min. Her thyroid is firm and twice normal size but not tender. Free T4 is high and TSH is suppressed. Radioactive iodine uptake is very low, and TSH-receptor antibodies are negative.
oneliner: 26F + 6 wk postpartum + nervous, tremor, weight loss + painless firm goitre + high FT4, low TSH + very low iodine uptake + TSH-receptor Ab negative → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains her symptoms?

options.A: Stimulating antibodies against the TSH receptor
options.B: Leakage of stored hormone from a gland infiltrated by lymphocytes
options.C: A nodule making hormone on its own
options.E: Excess iodine driving new hormone synthesis

whyNot.A: **Graves**: high iodine uptake, TSH-receptor antibodies positive
whyNot.C: **Toxic adenoma**: a single hot nodule with high uptake
whyNot.D: **TSH would be high**, not suppressed
whyNot.E: **Jod-Basedow**: follows an iodine load; she had none

answer: Release of preformed hormone from a lymphocyte-damaged gland (postpartum thyroiditis)
why: **Painless thyroiditis after delivery + high T4 with very low iodine uptake** = postpartum thyroiditis. Lymphocytes **damage follicles, which leak stored hormone**; no new hormone is being made, so uptake is low. A hypothyroid phase often follows.
chain: Stored T4 and T3 leak out (uptake low)
Short thyrotoxic phase → often hypothyroid phase

idea.rule: Thyrotoxicosis with LOW iodine uptake = hormone leaking or coming from outside (thyroiditis, levothyroxine use), not overproduction.
also: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis: painful, after a virus, high ESR
Factitious thyrotoxicosis: low thyroglobulin

stem: In a study of the human pro-opiomelanocortin gene, a single mRNA is made and translated into one large precursor protein. The same precursor is later found as two separate hormones, ACTH and beta-lipotropin, in anterior pituitary corticotrophs. Sequencing shows only one mature transcript species from the gene.
oneliner: Experiment: POMC gene → one mRNA, one large precursor → ACTH + beta-lipotropin, only one transcript species → how are two hormones made?
ask: Which process best explains how two different hormones arise from this gene?

options.A: Alternative splicing producing two different mRNAs
options.B: Somatic rearrangement of the gene segments
options.C: Proteolytic cleavage of the precursor protein after translation
options.D: Methylation of the promoter in different cells
options.E: Editing of the mRNA to create a stop codon

whyNot.A: Would give **two mRNA species**; only one transcript exists
whyNot.B: **Gene rearrangement** is how B and T cells make receptors, not endocrine cells
whyNot.D: Methylation **switches a gene off or on**; it does not make two products from one protein
whyNot.E: RNA editing (e.g. **apoB-48**) changes the mRNA; here the mRNA is single and unchanged

answer: Post-translational cleavage of the POMC prohormone
why: **One mRNA, one precursor, two products** means the split happens **after translation**. Prohormone convertases cleave POMC into **ACTH** and **beta-lipotropin** (and, elsewhere, MSH and endorphin).

idea.rule: Peptide hormones are made as inactive prohormones and activated by post-translational cleavage.
also: Proinsulin is cleaved to insulin and C-peptide
Proglucagon gives glucagon in islets and GLP-1 in the gut
Beta-lipotropin gives beta-endorphin; POMC also gives alpha-MSH

stem: A 28-year-old woman at 16 weeks of pregnancy has routine thyroid tests. Total T4 is 50% above the non-pregnant range, while TSH is normal and free T4 is normal. She feels well, with a heart rate of 78/min, no tremor, and no goiter.
oneliner: 28F + 16 wk pregnant + total T4 high + TSH normal + free T4 normal + asymptomatic → why is total T4 high?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the raised total T4?

options.A: Stimulating antibodies against the TSH receptor
options.B: Estrogen-driven rise in hepatic thyroxine-binding globulin
options.C: Autonomous thyroid tissue in an ovarian tumor
options.E: Increased peripheral conversion of T4 to T3

whyNot.A: **Graves disease**: free T4 high, TSH suppressed, symptoms
whyNot.C: **Struma ovarii**: free T4 high and TSH suppressed; she is euthyroid
whyNot.D: Would give **high or inappropriately normal TSH with high free T4**; free T4 here is normal
whyNot.E: Would **lower** T4 and not change binding protein; total T4 is raised

answer: Raised thyroxine-binding globulin from estrogen
why: **Estrogen** in pregnancy **increases hepatic TBG synthesis** and slows its clearance. More binding protein holds more **total T4**, but **free T4 and TSH stay normal**, so she is euthyroid.

idea.rule: High total T4 with normal TSH and free T4 means more binding protein, not more hormone.
also: Estrogen, oral contraceptives, hepatitis raise TBG
Androgens, glucocorticoids, nephrotic syndrome lower TBG
Free hormone is the active fraction, so the axis is unchanged

stem: A 13-year-old girl in a rapid growth spurt has a balance study showing intestinal calcium absorption well above the adult fraction. Her serum calcium and PTH are normal, and she has regular sun exposure.
oneliner: 13F + growth spurt + gut calcium absorption high + normal Ca and PTH + sun exposure → which hormone?
ask: Which hormone most directly increases her intestinal calcium absorption?

options.C: Parathyroid hormone acting directly on enterocytes

whyNot.A: Lowers serum calcium by **inhibiting osteoclasts**; no gut effect
whyNot.B: **Reduces** intestinal calcium absorption (and bone formation)
whyNot.C: PTH acts on bone and kidney; its gut effect is **indirect, via calcitriol**; her PTH is normal
whyNot.E: Acts on the **collecting duct** for sodium and potassium

answer: Calcitriol made from skin 7-dehydrocholesterol
why: Sunlight converts **7-dehydrocholesterol** to vitamin D3; **liver 25-hydroxylation** and **renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation** give **calcitriol**. It induces **calbindin** and apical channels in enterocytes, raising calcium uptake to meet growth demands.
chain: Calbindin and calcium channels in enterocytes

idea.rule: Calcitriol is the hormone that drives intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption.
also: PTH raises renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so it acts on the gut indirectly
Growth, pregnancy and lactation raise calcitriol
Sarcoidosis makes calcitriol in granulomas

stem: A 54-year-old man has a serum cortisol three times his baseline on the first morning after a long abdominal operation. He has had no steroids. The rise was driven by a pituitary hormone that stimulates the zona fasciculata.
oneliner: 54M + day 1 after major surgery + cortisol ×3 + no steroids + pituitary hormone drives zona fasciculata → which cell?
ask: Which cell type released the hormone that directly stimulated his adrenal cortex?

options.A: Acidophilic cells of the anterior pituitary
options.D: Basophilic thyrotrophs of the anterior pituitary
options.E: Basophilic corticotrophs of the anterior pituitary

whyNot.A: Make **growth hormone and prolactin**, not ACTH
whyNot.B: Glial cells; **ADH and oxytocin** are made in the hypothalamus and stored in axon terminals here, not ACTH
whyNot.C: Release **CRH**, which acts on the pituitary, **not directly on the adrenal**
whyNot.D: Basophils too, but they make **TSH**, which acts on the thyroid

answer: Corticotrophs (basophils) releasing ACTH
why: **Surgical stress** triggers hypothalamic **CRH**, which makes **corticotrophs** release **ACTH**. ACTH acts on the **zona fasciculata** to raise cortisol. Corticotrophs stain **basophilic** because POMC is glycosylated.

idea.rule: ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH come from basophils; GH and prolactin come from acidophils.
also: Mnemonic B-FLAT: basophils make FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH
Acidophils: GH and prolactin
Posterior pituitary stores hormones made in hypothalamus

stem: A newborn girl has hyperglycemia from the first day of life. Imaging shows an absent pancreatic body and tail with no detectable insulin. A transcription factor needed for pancreatic bud formation is mutated.
oneliner: Newborn F + hyperglycemia day 1 + no insulin + absent pancreas + bud transcription factor mutated → islet cells derive from which tissue?
ask: From which embryonic tissue do the islet cells normally arise?

whyNot.B: Gives **primordial germ cells**, not pancreatic cells
whyNot.C: Gives **melanocytes, adrenal medulla, ganglia**
whyNot.D: Forms **somites** (skeletal muscle, vertebrae)
whyNot.E: Forms the **gut wall muscle and connective tissue**, not the glandular cells

answer: Foregut endoderm (dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds)
why: The pancreas grows as **dorsal and ventral buds from foregut endoderm**. Both the **exocrine glands and the islets** differentiate from that endoderm, so failed endodermal bud development removes insulin-producing cells.

idea.rule: Gut-tube epithelium and its glands come from endoderm; the wall and connective tissue come from splanchnic mesoderm.
also: Liver, gallbladder and pancreas all bud from the foregut
Annular pancreas: ventral bud wraps the duodenum
Pancreas divisum: buds fail to fuse

stem: Isolated pancreatic islets are perfused with a high-glucose solution, and insulin appears in the outflow within minutes. Removing extracellular calcium abolishes the release. Electron microscopy at peak release shows dense-core granules fused with the beta-cell plasma membrane.
oneliner: Experiment: islets + high glucose → insulin out in minutes + abolished without extracellular Ca + granules fused with membrane on EM → how is insulin released?
ask: Which process best describes how insulin leaves the beta cell?

options.A: Simple diffusion across the plasma membrane
options.B: Facilitated diffusion through a GLUT transporter
options.D: Secondary active transport coupled to sodium

whyNot.A: Insulin is a **large, polar peptide** that cannot cross a lipid bilayer
whyNot.B: **GLUT2 carries glucose into** the cell; insulin is a peptide, not a sugar
whyNot.D: Insulin is not a carrier substrate; release needs **extracellular calcium** and **granule fusion**
whyNot.E: Endocytosis **takes material in**; the granules here are fusing outward

answer: Calcium-triggered exocytosis of insulin granules
why: **Glucose enters via GLUT2**, ATP rises and closes **ATP-sensitive K+ channels**. The cell **depolarizes**, **voltage-gated calcium channels open**, and calcium triggers **granule exocytosis** of insulin and C-peptide.
chain: Granules fuse with membrane and release insulin

idea.rule: Peptide hormones leave endocrine cells by calcium-dependent vesicle exocytosis, not diffusion.
also: Sulfonylureas close KATP channels to force insulin release
Diazoxide opens KATP channels and lowers insulin
Steroid hormones do diffuse out, being lipid soluble

stem: A 28-year-old man has had palpitations, tremor and heat intolerance for 2 months. His thyroid is diffusely enlarged with a bruit. Free T4 is elevated and TSH is below 0.03 µU/mL.
oneliner: 28M + palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance + diffuse goiter with bruit + high T4 + TSH <0.03 → what does the autoantibody bind?
ask: His disease is caused by autoantibodies that most likely bind to which of the following?

whyNot.A: **Anti-T4** antibodies cause assay artifact, not hyperthyroidism
whyNot.B: Located on **pituitary thyrotrophs**; stimulating it would **raise** TSH
whyNot.C: Antibodies against it would lower TSH and **cause hypothyroidism**
whyNot.D: Antibodies against TSH would cause **hypothyroidism**, not hyperthyroidism

answer: Stimulating antibodies bind the TSH receptor
why: **Graves disease** is a **type II hypersensitivity**. The autoantibodies **mimic TSH** at the thyroid **TSH receptor**, driving T4/T3 production and thyroid growth. **TSH is suppressed** by negative feedback.
chain: T4 and T3 rise, goiter forms

idea.rule: In some type II hypersensitivity diseases the antibody acts on a receptor instead of destroying the cell.
also: Graves: antibody stimulates the TSH receptor
Myasthenia gravis: antibody blocks the acetylcholine receptor
Neonatal Graves from transplacental IgG

stem: A 56-year-old man has lost 9 kg over 6 months. He has a painful, migrating red rash with crusting on his legs and around his mouth, and new diabetes with a glucose of 280 mg/dL. Serum glucagon is 1,500 pg/mL, and CT shows a mass in the pancreas.
oneliner: 56M + weight loss + migrating crusting rash + new diabetes + glucagon 1500 + pancreatic mass → which hepatic effect drives ketone production?
ask: Which of the following hepatic effects of this hormone excess most directly promotes ketone formation?

options.E: Increased fatty acid entry into mitochondria and beta-oxidation

whyNot.A: Glucagon **inhibits** glycogen synthesis and stimulates breakdown
whyNot.B: Glucagon **inhibits** this enzyme, which lowers malonyl-CoA
whyNot.C: That would **block** fatty acid entry and ketogenesis
whyNot.D: Glucagon **lowers** fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, slowing glycolysis

answer: Glucagon lowers malonyl-CoA, freeing fatty acid entry to mitochondria
why: **Glucagon raises cAMP** and PKA, which **inhibit acetyl-CoA carboxylase**, so **malonyl-CoA falls** and carnitine acyltransferase I is released. Fatty acids enter mitochondria, **beta-oxidation rises** and **acetyl-CoA** is diverted to ketone bodies.
chain: cAMP and PKA rise in liver

idea.rule: Glucagon promotes glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis, and inhibits glycogen synthesis and glycolysis.
also: Fasting and DKA: high glucagon-to-insulin ratio drives ketone production
Insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, raising malonyl-CoA and blocking CPT-I
Glucagon lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, favoring gluconeogenesis

stem: A 38-year-old woman has weight gain, purple abdominal striae, hypertension and easy bruising. Plasma ACTH is below 5 pg/mL. Her cortisol does not fall after low-dose or high-dose dexamethasone. CT shows a 4-cm right adrenal mass and a thin left adrenal gland.
oneliner: 38F + weight gain + purple striae + hypertension + ACTH <5 + no cortisol suppression on low or high dexamethasone + 4-cm right adrenal mass, thin left adrenal → source of excess cortisol?
ask: Which origin of excess cortisol best fits?

options.C: Autonomous cortisol-secreting tumor of the adrenal zona fasciculata
options.D: Aldosterone-producing tumor of the zona glomerulosa
options.E: Androgen-producing tumor of the zona reticularis

whyNot.A: ACTH would be **high** and the adrenals would be enlarged on both sides
whyNot.B: ACTH would be **high or normal** and cortisol would **suppress on high-dose** dexamethasone
whyNot.D: Gives **hypertension with low K**, not Cushingoid features
whyNot.E: Would cause **virilization**, not striae with high cortisol

answer: ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome from an adrenal tumor
why: **ACTH is suppressed** because autonomous cortisol shuts off the pituitary by negative feedback; the **other adrenal atrophies**. Cortisol is **not suppressed by dexamethasone** because the tumor ignores ACTH. The **zona fasciculata** makes cortisol.
chain: Negative feedback suppresses CRH and ACTH

idea.rule: Cushing syndrome with low ACTH = adrenal tumor or exogenous glucocorticoid.
also: Exogenous steroids are the most common cause overall
Pituitary adenoma: suppresses on high-dose dexamethasone
Ectopic ACTH: no suppression, high ACTH, often small cell lung cancer

stem: A 9-year-old boy has had 3 weeks of thirst, frequent urination and weight loss. He now has vomiting and deep rapid breathing, his breath smells fruity, and he is difficult to rouse. Skin tenting is present and blood pressure is low. Glucose is 560 mg/dL, pH is 7.05 and serum osmolality is 340 mOsm/kg.
oneliner: 9M + 3 wk thirst, polyuria, weight loss + vomiting, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath + hard to rouse + skin tenting, low BP + glucose 560, pH 7.05, osmolality 340 → why is he drowsy?
ask: Which mechanism most likely explains his depressed consciousness?

options.A: Increased oxygen affinity of glycated hemoglobin
options.B: Severe dehydration and hyperosmolality from glucose-driven osmotic diuresis
options.C: Failure of glucose to cross the blood-brain barrier
options.D: Fatty acids accumulating in cerebrospinal fluid
options.E: Neurons unable to use glucose because they lack insulin

whyNot.A: Glycation is **slow and minor**; this is an acute event
whyNot.C: Brain glucose uptake is **insulin independent** and he has very high glucose
whyNot.D: Fatty acids are **protein-bound** and do not cross freely
whyNot.E: Neurons use **GLUT3 independent of insulin**

answer: Hyperosmolar dehydration of the brain and body (with acidosis) from osmotic diuresis
why: **Insulin lack makes glucose very high**; glucose spills into urine and **pulls out water (osmotic diuresis)**. The **extreme hyperosmolality and volume loss** impair brain function, with **ketoacidosis** adding to it.

idea.rule: In DKA, mental status tracks effective osmolality and volume loss.
also: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state: osmolality above 320 gives coma with little acidosis
Hypernatremia: brain cells shrink, confusion
Correcting osmolality too fast in children: cerebral edema

stem: A 15-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes takes extra insulin and has a glucose of 40 mg/dL at 3 AM, when he is sweaty and trembling. His symptoms settle without eating, and at 7 AM his glucose is 290 mg/dL.
oneliner: 15M + type 1 diabetes + extra insulin + glucose 40 at 3 AM with sweating, tremor + 290 at 7 AM without food → mechanism of the rebound?
ask: Which of the following best explains the rise in glucose?

options.D: Activation of hepatic adenylyl cyclase by glucagon and epinephrine
options.E: Inhibition of hepatic protein kinase A

whyNot.A: Would **store** glucose in muscle, lowering blood glucose
whyNot.B: Muscle lacks **glucose-6-phosphatase** and cannot release glucose to blood
whyNot.C: Would favor **glycogen synthesis**, not release
whyNot.E: Would **block** glycogenolysis

answer: Counterregulatory hormones raise hepatic cAMP, causing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
why: Hypoglycemia triggers **glucagon and epinephrine**, which bind G-protein receptors on hepatocytes to activate **adenylyl cyclase**, **raise cAMP and PKA**, and drive **glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis**. The liver, not muscle, releases glucose.
chain: Hepatic adenylyl cyclase, cAMP and PKA up

idea.rule: Liver releases glucose; muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and glucagon receptors.
also: Epinephrine causes the tremor and sweating
Cortisol and growth hormone act later
Hypoglycemia unawareness in long-standing diabetes
Dawn phenomenon: rise from hormones without a preceding low

stem: A 44-year-old man has had hypertension for 6 years despite three drugs, with muscle weakness and nocturia. Blood pressure is 172/104 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 2.1 mEq/L and bicarbonate 33 mEq/L. Plasma aldosterone is high and plasma renin activity is undetectable. Urinary free cortisol is normal and ACTH is low-normal.
oneliner: 44M + resistant hypertension + weakness + K 2.1, HCO3 33 + aldosterone high, renin undetectable + normal cortisol → why low K and alkalosis?
ask: Which of the following best explains his electrolyte findings?

options.A: Excess cortisol saturating the mineralocorticoid receptor
options.B: Autonomous aldosterone raising distal sodium reabsorption and potassium and H+ secretion
options.C: Catecholamine-driven shift of potassium into cells

whyNot.A: **Urinary cortisol is normal**, and aldosterone would be low
whyNot.C: Does not explain **alkalosis, high aldosterone and persistent hypertension**
whyNot.D: That would give **high potassium and acidosis**
whyNot.E: Reduced GFR gives **hyperkalemia**, not low K

answer: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn): aldosterone excess independent of renin
why: The adrenal makes **aldosterone on its own**. It drives **Na+ reabsorption (volume expansion, hypertension)** with **K+ and H+ loss** in the collecting duct. The expanded volume **suppresses renin**.
chain: Adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia secretes aldosterone
Na+ retention and ENaC activity rise
K+ and H+ lost in urine

idea.rule: Hypertension + hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis + low renin = primary aldosteronism.
also: Screening: aldosterone-to-renin ratio
Edema is absent because of aldosterone escape
Treat adenoma by surgery, bilateral disease with spironolactone
Secondary hyperaldosteronism has high renin (renal artery stenosis)

stem: A 46-year-old woman has episodes of pounding headache, sweating and palpitations, with labile hypertension. A CT shows a 4-cm right adrenal mass and plasma metanephrines are 12 times normal. She has no abdominal or flank pain. In the emergency department for a fast heart rate, she is given intravenous propranolol. Within 30 minutes her blood pressure rises from 160/96 to 250/150 mm Hg.
oneliner: 46F + paroxysms of headache, sweating, palpitations + labile HTN + 4 cm adrenal mass + metanephrines ×12 + IV propranolol → BP 160/96 to 250/150 → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains the rise in blood pressure?

options.D: Infarction of the tumor with a sudden release

whyNot.A: Does not explain the **abrupt rise precisely after the drug** in a patient with a catecholamine tumor
whyNot.B: Propranolol does **not inhibit COMT or MAO**
whyNot.C: Beta-1 blockade **lowers** renin release, and it could not raise pressure this fast
whyNot.D: Bleeding into the tumor gives **flank or abdominal pain**, which she lacks; the surge followed **the drug**

answer: Beta blockade unmasks alpha-1 vasoconstriction
why: Catecholamines normally act on **beta-2 receptors (vasodilation)** and **alpha-1 receptors (vasoconstriction)**. **Blocking beta-2 with propranolol** removes the vasodilation, leaving **alpha-1 effect unopposed** and causing a hypertensive crisis. An **alpha-blocker comes first**.

idea.rule: In pheochromocytoma give an alpha-blocker (phenoxybenzamine) before any beta-blocker.
also: Phenoxybenzamine (irreversible) for 10 to 14 days before surgery
Same trap: beta-blocker alone in cocaine toxicity
Labetalol has some alpha block but is not the first step
Volume loading after alpha blockade prevents postoperative hypotension

stem: A 63-year-old man who smokes has 3 months of cough and weight loss. He has darkened skin, proximal muscle weakness, blood pressure 168/100 mm Hg, potassium 2.7 mEq/L and glucose 210 mg/dL. Plasma ACTH is 180 pg/mL (high) and cortisol is high. Cortisol is not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone. A CT shows a central hilar lung mass, and pituitary MRI is normal.
oneliner: 63M + smoker + cough, weight loss + hyperpigmentation, proximal weakness + BP 168/100, K 2.7, glucose 210 + ACTH high + cortisol not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone + hilar mass, normal pituitary MRI → source?
ask: Which of the following best explains his hormone findings?

options.C: Ectopic ACTH secretion by the lung tumor

whyNot.A: Usually **suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone**, and his **pituitary MRI is normal**
whyNot.B: ACTH would be **low**, not 180
whyNot.D: Gives **low ACTH** and no tumor
whyNot.E: CRH excess drives the **pituitary**, which still suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone; his does not, and the **pituitary MRI is normal**

answer: Paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome: ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer
why: A **central hilar mass in a smoker** with **very high ACTH** and **no dexamethasone suppression** means tumor-derived ACTH, usually **small cell carcinoma**. The tumor has **no cortisol feedback**; high cortisol saturates renal 11-beta-HSD2, giving **hypokalemia and hypertension**.
chain: Small cell lung cancer makes ACTH

idea.rule: Cushing syndrome with very high ACTH and no suppression by high-dose dexamethasone = ectopic ACTH.
also: Pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone
Adrenal tumor: ACTH low
Other ectopic ACTH: carcinoid, medullary thyroid carcinoma
Hyperpigmentation comes from ACTH and MSH fragments

stem: A 48-year-old woman has a kidney stone and a serum calcium of 11.9 mg/dL. Her phosphate is low, intact PTH is raised, and 24-hour urine calcium is high. She takes no supplements and has no gut disease.
oneliner: 48F + kidney stone + Ca 11.9 + low phosphate + high PTH + high urine Ca → how is her gut absorbing extra calcium?
ask: Which step best explains her increased intestinal calcium absorption?

options.A: PTH binding directly to enterocyte receptors
options.B: Hepatic hydroxylation of vitamin D to 25-OH vitamin D
options.C: PTH-driven renal conversion of 25-OH vitamin D to calcitriol
options.E: Skin synthesis of cholecalciferol under ultraviolet light

whyNot.A: The gut has **no significant PTH effect**; PTH acts on bone and kidney, and gut absorption is indirect
whyNot.B: The **liver step is not PTH-regulated**; the renal 1-alpha step is
whyNot.D: **Calcitonin lowers** calcium (bone), and is not the driver of absorption
whyNot.E: Not controlled by PTH; **no change in sun exposure** is described

answer: PTH stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, raising calcitriol
why: PTH **induces 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the proximal tubule**, so more 25-OH vitamin D becomes **calcitriol**. Calcitriol raises **intestinal calcium absorption**; PTH itself does not act on the gut.

idea.rule: PTH reaches the gut only through calcitriol.
also: PTH on bone: osteoclast activation via RANKL
PTH on kidney: more calcium reabsorption, less phosphate reabsorption
Low phosphate comes from phosphaturia

stem: A 41-year-old man has bone pain, polyuria and constant thirst. He has had two duodenal ulcers in the past three years. His serum calcium is 13.5 mg/dL and intact PTH is raised. A hand x-ray shows subperiosteal resorption along the phalanges. His urine calcium is high.
oneliner: 41M + bone pain + polyuria and thirst + recurrent duodenal ulcers + Ca 13.5 + high PTH + subperiosteal resorption → what raises his calcium?
ask: Which process is most responsible for the rise in his serum calcium?

options.E: Increased osteoclast activity and bone resorption

whyNot.A: PTH **increases** distal tubule calcium reabsorption; reduced reabsorption would lower calcium
whyNot.B: Calcitonin **lowers** calcium and is not elevated to cause hypercalcemia
whyNot.C: This would **lower** serum calcium; PTH raises calcitriol and absorption
whyNot.D: Deposition **removes** calcium from blood; the x-ray shows resorption

answer: PTH-driven osteoclast activation releases calcium from bone
why: A PTH-secreting adenoma (ulcers suggest **MEN1**) acts on **osteoblasts to raise RANKL**, which activates osteoclasts. **Bone resorption** (subperiosteal erosions, bone pain) pours calcium into blood and the high load causes polyuria.

idea.rule: Chronic excess PTH takes calcium from bone to keep blood calcium up.
also: Osteitis fibrosa cystica: brown tumours, subperiosteal erosions
Secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD: same bone loss (renal osteodystrophy)
PTHrP from squamous cell carcinoma resorbs bone the same way

stem: A 3-day-old newborn has fused labioscrotal folds and an enlarged phallus-like clitoris, with no palpable gonads. The karyotype is 46,XX and ultrasound shows a uterus and ovaries. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone is markedly raised. The mother took no hormones in pregnancy and was not virilized.
oneliner: 3-day-old + ambiguous genitalia + 46,XX + uterus and ovaries + high 17-OHP + mother not virilized → why virilized?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the virilization?

options.D: Low cortisol raises ACTH, driving precursors into androgen synthesis

whyNot.A: **Mother would be virilized** in pregnancy, and 17-OHP is not raised
whyNot.B: **AIS** has a 46,XY karyotype and no uterus
whyNot.C: Very rare in a neonate and **17-OHP would not be elevated**
whyNot.E: **No maternal hormones** and the mother was not virilized; 17-OHP would not be raised

answer: 21-hydroxylase block: cortisol low, ACTH high, androgens in excess
why: A **21-hydroxylase block** stops cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, so **ACTH rises** and **17-OH progesterone piles up**. Precursors flow down the **androgen pathway**, **virilizing a female fetus** while internal structures stay female.

idea.rule: High 17-OH progesterone is the hallmark of 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
also: Salt wasting: low aldosterone, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia
11-beta-hydroxylase: virilization plus hypertension
17-alpha-hydroxylase: hypertension, no sex steroids

stem: A 34-year-old man is running a marathon. Around mile 20 he has marked muscle pain and fatigue, then he suddenly feels euphoric, with his pain fading. Heart rate and blood pressure are stable and he has no palpitations or tremor.
oneliner: 34M + marathon mile 20 + severe muscle pain then sudden euphoria with pain relief + no tremor, palpitations → which substance?
ask: Which of the following substances most likely mediates this effect?

whyNot.A: Stimulates adrenal cortisol; **no direct analgesic or euphoric action**
whyNot.B: Would cause **tachycardia, tremor, anxiety**, not pain relief
whyNot.C: Raises blood glucose; **no CNS or analgesic effect**
whyNot.E: Inhibits hormone secretion; **no euphoria**

answer: Beta-endorphin released with prolonged exercise
why: Sustained intense exercise and pain release **beta-endorphin**, an endogenous opioid cleaved from **POMC** in the pituitary. It acts on **mu opioid receptors**, causing analgesia and euphoria (the 'runner's high').
chain: Binds mu opioid receptors in the CNS

idea.rule: Pain and sustained stress release beta-endorphin, an endogenous opioid cut from POMC, giving analgesia.
also: Stress-induced analgesia after injury
Endorphin release with acupuncture
Enkephalins gating pain in the dorsal horn

stem: Healthy volunteers rest in a laboratory. A hypertonic mannitol infusion raises plasma osmolality from 285 to 300 mOsm/kg H₂O without a change in blood pressure or heart rate. Mannitol stays in the extracellular space. Plasma ADH is measured every 15 minutes.
oneliner: Volunteers + hypertonic mannitol infusion + plasma osmolality 285 → 300 + BP and HR unchanged → what happens to ADH and why?
ask: Which of the following best describes the ADH response?

options.A: Increased, because hypothalamic osmoreceptor cells shrink as water leaves them
options.B: Unchanged, because mannitol equilibrates across cell membranes
options.D: Increased, because baroreceptors sense a low pressure

whyNot.B: Mannitol **stays outside cells** (stated); crossing membranes freely is what **urea** does
whyNot.C: Volume change is **small** here; the osmotic signal is stronger
whyNot.D: BP and HR are **unchanged**
whyNot.E: Cells **shrink**, not swell, in a hypertonic environment

answer: Increased ADH, from osmoreceptor shrinkage
why: Mannitol is an **effective osmole**: it stays extracellular and draws water out of cells. **Hypothalamic osmoreceptors shrink**, and ADH release rises, ahead of any change in blood pressure.

idea.rule: Only effective osmoles (confined outside cells) move water and drive ADH; urea does not.
also: Hypernatremia and hyperglycemia
Water deprivation
Osmoreceptor sensitivity: a 1 to 2% rise triggers ADH

stem: A newly isolated hormone is a water-soluble peptide of 51 amino acids. When applied to cultured hepatocytes, glucose output changes within minutes. The effect appears even when transcription is blocked with actinomycin D.
oneliner: Water-soluble 51-aa peptide hormone + hepatocytes respond in minutes + effect persists with transcription blocked → receptor type and onset?
ask: Which of the following best describes its receptor, speed of action and a hormone of the same class?

options.B: Cell membrane receptor, slow onset, insulin
options.D: Nuclear receptor, slow onset, thyroid hormone
options.E: Cell membrane receptor, rapid onset, insulin

whyNot.A: Needs lipid solubility to enter the cell; **speed here is minutes**
whyNot.B: The response occurs **within minutes**, so it is not slow
whyNot.C: A water-soluble peptide **cannot cross** the membrane to a nuclear receptor
whyNot.D: Acts on **gene transcription**, which is blocked here but the effect persists

answer: Peptide hormones use membrane receptors with fast second messenger signaling
why: A **water-soluble peptide cannot cross the plasma membrane**, so it binds a **cell surface receptor** and acts through second messengers or kinase cascades, with a **rapid onset**. The effect persisting with transcription blocked excludes a nuclear receptor.

idea.rule: Water-soluble hormones act at the cell surface quickly; lipid-soluble hormones act in the nucleus slowly.
also: Glucagon and PTH (cAMP)
Insulin (receptor tyrosine kinase)
ADH and oxytocin (G protein-coupled receptors)
Catecholamines act on cell surface receptors despite small size

stem: In pancreatic beta cells, proinsulin folds in the endoplasmic reticulum and is packaged into secretory granules. There, prohormone convertases excise the C-peptide. The mature A and B chains nonetheless stay joined to each other by covalent bonds.
oneliner: Beta-cell proinsulin → C-peptide cleaved → A and B chains remain covalently joined → which residues form the link?
ask: Which of the following amino acids forms the covalent bonds joining the A and B chains?

whyNot.A: Carries a positively charged amine; forms **ionic and amide** links, not interchain covalent bridges here
whyNot.B: Has a thioether side chain that **cannot form** a covalent bond with another residue
whyNot.D: Hydroxyl group forms **phosphate esters**, not disulfides
whyNot.E: Phenol side chain; can be phosphorylated but **does not link chains**

answer: Cysteine (disulfide bonds)
why: Pairs of **cysteine** residues are oxidized in the ER to **disulfide bonds**, which fold proinsulin correctly and keep the A and B chains linked after C-peptide is removed.
chain: Cysteine thiols oxidize to disulfide bonds
A and B chains stay linked by disulfides

idea.rule: Disulfide bonds between cysteines stabilize secreted proteins.
also: Antibody heavy and light chains
Keratin in hair (permanent waving breaks these bonds)
Collagen propeptides
Extracellular domains of membrane receptors

stem: A healthy 25-year-old woman has free access to food but keeps a fixed routine, eating lunch at 12:30 PM. Blood is drawn for plasma ghrelin every 30 minutes through the day. Her last food was breakfast at 7:30 AM.
oneliner: 25F + free access to food, lunch at 12:30 + ghrelin sampled q30 min all day → when is ghrelin highest?
ask: At which of the following times is plasma ghrelin most likely highest?

whyNot.A: Ghrelin **falls** once food reaches the gut
whyNot.B: Still **suppressed** after a meal
whyNot.C: Rising, but **not yet at the peak**
whyNot.E: A **post-meal** nadir

answer: Preprandial peak of ghrelin
why: **Ghrelin** is made by the **empty stomach** (gastric X/A-like cells) and rises through the fast to peak **just before the meal**, stimulating hunger via the hypothalamus. Food in the gut **suppresses** it.

idea.rule: Ghrelin is the hunger hormone: high when empty, suppressed by food.
also: Rises with sleep deprivation
Prader-Willi syndrome has very high ghrelin
Rises during dieting-induced weight loss

stem: A 13-year-old girl is in her pubertal growth spurt, growing 8 cm/year. A calcium balance study on a constant diet without supplements shows intestinal calcium absorption has risen from 25% to 40% of intake. Serum calcium is normal, and she gets regular sun exposure.
oneliner: 13F + growth spurt 8 cm/y + intestinal Ca absorption 25 → 40% + normal serum Ca + good sun exposure → what raises absorption?
ask: Which of the following best explains the increased calcium absorption?

options.C: Parathyroid hormone acting directly on enterocytes

whyNot.B: **Lowers** serum calcium and does not drive absorption
whyNot.C: PTH acts on **bone and kidney**; it raises gut absorption only through calcitriol
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids **reduce** calcium absorption
whyNot.E: Glucagon has **no role** in calcium handling

answer: Calcitriol (made via skin 7-dehydrocholesterol, liver and kidney)
why: Growth raises calcium demand, so renal **1-alpha-hydroxylase** makes more **calcitriol** from skin 7-dehydrocholesterol. Calcitriol induces **calbindin and TRPV6** in enterocytes, raising intestinal calcium absorption.

idea.rule: Calcitriol is the hormone that raises intestinal calcium (and phosphate) absorption.
also: Pregnancy and lactation
Hypocalcemia (via PTH)
Granulomatous disease (macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase)
Low-calcium diet (adaptive rise)

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 30 weeks of gestation has total serum cortisol three times the upper limit of normal. She has no striae beyond those expected, no muscle wasting, easy bruising or hyperglycemia, and her blood pressure and weight gain are appropriate. She takes no medications.
oneliner: 30F + 30 weeks pregnant + total cortisol ×3 + no Cushingoid or catabolic features, normal glucose and BP → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains the absence of catabolic effects?

whyNot.A: Would be **autoimmune** and not explain a pregnancy pattern
whyNot.B: Would **lower** the total cortisol, not raise it
whyNot.C: No sign of **resistance**; the pregnancy cause is binding
whyNot.D: Cortisol is lipophilic and **freely crosses** the membrane

answer: Estrogen-driven rise in corticosteroid-binding globulin
why: Placental estrogen makes the liver produce more **CBG**, so **total cortisol rises but most is protein-bound and inactive**. The free fraction stays relatively low, so there are few catabolic effects.
chain: Total cortisol rises; free hormone effect limited

idea.rule: Only free hormone is active, so binding-protein changes alter total levels without proportionate effect.
also: Oral contraceptives (raise CBG)
Estrogen therapy
Pregnancy raises thyroxine-binding globulin too (total T4 up, free T4 normal)
Nephrotic syndrome lowers binding proteins

stem: A 44-year-old man with a BMI of 43 kg/m² and prediabetes is scheduled for Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. His dietitian tells him which kind of food to avoid afterward, because within 30 minutes it can cause flushing, palpitations, cramping and diarrhea.
oneliner: 44M + BMI 43 + prediabetes + pre-op counseling for Roux-en-Y bypass → which food provokes flushing, palpitations, cramps, diarrhea soon after eating?
ask: Which of the following foods is most likely to cause these symptoms after surgery?

whyNot.A: Protein is **slowly** digested and not strongly osmotic
whyNot.B: Low in calories and sugar; **not** osmotically active
whyNot.C: High in fat and protein; **slow** to hydrolyze
whyNot.E: Mostly protein, **not** a carbohydrate load

answer: Refined starchy foods
why: After bypass the **pylorus is bypassed** and refined carbohydrate is dumped into the small bowel. It is hydrolyzed to sugar that is **hyperosmolar**, so fluid shifts into the lumen, causing **early dumping**: flushing, tachycardia, cramps and diarrhea.
chain: Hyperosmolar carbohydrate reaches the small bowel
Later: glucose spike then rebound hypoglycemia

idea.rule: Rapid emptying of osmotic carbohydrate into the small bowel causes dumping.
also: Gastric bypass and gastrectomy
Esophagectomy with gastric pull-up
Vagotomy with pyloroplasty
Late dumping is reactive hypoglycemia 1 to 3 hours after meal

stem: A 54-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 25 years has progressive renal failure with a creatinine of 5.8 mg/dL and is not yet on dialysis. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL, MCV is 88 fL, reticulocyte count is low, and ferritin and B12 are normal. There is no bleeding and her smear shows no fragments.
oneliner: 54F + type 1 DM + progressive renal failure, pre-dialysis + Hb 8.9, MCV 88 + low reticulocytes → why anemic?
ask: What is the most likely mechanism of her anemia?

options.A: Acute loss of red cells through bleeding
options.E: Impaired DNA synthesis in red cell precursors

whyNot.A: Stem states **no bleeding** and a **low** reticulocyte count
whyNot.B: Would give **raised reticulocytes** and spherocytes
whyNot.C: Gives **microcytosis or ring sideroblasts**; MCV here is normal
whyNot.E: **Megaloblastic** (high MCV); B12 is normal

answer: Erythropoietin deficiency
why: Peritubular interstitial cells of the **kidney** make **erythropoietin**. With failing kidneys the marrow gets less stimulus, producing a **normocytic, normochromic anemia** with a low reticulocyte count.
chain: Chronic kidney disease destroys EPO-making cells

idea.rule: The kidney senses O2 and makes EPO; failing kidneys cause a hypoproliferative normocytic anemia.
also: Chronic renal failure (treated with ESA)
Bilateral nephrectomy
Diabetic nephropathy

stem: A 12-year-old girl is newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. Her father and a paternal aunt also have the disease. A counsellor wants a molecular marker to identify which relatives carry inherited risk.
oneliner: 12F + new type 1 DM + father and aunt affected → which gene products mark inherited risk?
ask: Typing for which molecules would be most useful?

whyNot.A: Co-receptor with **no** disease-linked polymorphism useful for typing
whyNot.B: Co-receptor **without** disease-linked inherited variation
whyNot.C: Each B cell makes a **different** antibody by rearrangement, so there is no inherited marker
whyNot.D: Also **rearranged**, unique per clone

answer: Histocompatibility (HLA) antigens
why: Many autoimmune diseases are linked to particular **HLA alleles** (type 1 diabetes: **HLA-DR3 and DR4**). HLA is **highly polymorphic** and inherited, so typing flags relatives at higher risk.
chain: HLA genes are highly polymorphic and inherited
DR3/DR4 alleles present islet self-peptides to autoreactive T cells

idea.rule: Inherited autoimmune risk is carried mainly by particular HLA alleles.
also: Type 1 diabetes (HLA-DR3, DR4)
Ankylosing spondylitis (HLA-B27)
Rheumatoid arthritis (HLA-DR4)
Celiac disease (HLA-DQ2, DQ8)
Multiple sclerosis (HLA-DR2)

stem: A 12-year-old boy has early testicular enlargement and mild acne. He is Tanner stage 2, with height and weight at the 50th percentile. Scrotal skin is thinned and testes are 5 mL.
oneliner: 12M + Tanner 2 + testes 5 mL + thin scrotal skin + mild acne → what starts normal puberty?
ask: Which change marks the onset of normal male puberty?

options.B: Falling number of pituitary GnRH receptors
options.C: Loss of inhibin B from Sertoli cells

whyNot.A: Puberty needs **pulses**; continuous GnRH **desensitizes** the pituitary
whyNot.B: Receptor loss would **lower** gonadotropins
whyNot.C: Inhibin is not the **trigger**; it follows Sertoli maturation
whyNot.E: Autonomous testosterone is **peripheral precocity**, with small testes

answer: Nocturnal pulsatile LH secretion
why: Puberty begins when the **GnRH pulse generator reactivates**, giving **pulses of LH during sleep**. LH drives Leydig cell testosterone, which causes secondary sexual traits.

idea.rule: Normal puberty is pulsatile GnRH/LH, first at night; continuous GnRH shuts the axis down.
also: Kallmann syndrome: no GnRH pulses, so puberty is absent
Continuous leuprolide suppresses LH and FSH
Pulsatile GnRH restores ovulation in hypothalamic amenorrhea

stem: A 30-year-old woman has weight loss, heat intolerance and palpitations. Examination shows a diffusely enlarged, nontender thyroid, lid retraction with protruding eyes and pretibial swelling. Her TSH is suppressed and radioiodine uptake is diffusely increased. She has antibodies that bind the TSH receptor.
oneliner: 30F + weight loss, heat intolerance + diffuse goiter + exophthalmos, pretibial swelling + low TSH, high diffuse uptake + anti-TSH receptor antibodies → which hypersensitivity type?
ask: Which hypersensitivity mechanism does her disease share with Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn?

options.A: Type I: IgE on mast cells
options.B: Type II: IgG against a cell-surface target
options.C: Type III: circulating immune complexes deposited in tissue
options.D: Type IV: CD4+ T cells activating macrophages
options.E: Anaphylactoid: direct mast cell activation without antibody

whyNot.A: **Type I** uses IgE on mast cells for immediate allergy; her antibody acts on a **thyroid receptor**
whyNot.C: **Type III** complexes deposit in vessels and joints; her antibody binds the **TSH receptor** directly
whyNot.D: **Type IV** delayed T-cell reactions, such as the tuberculin test, need no antibody; hers is **antibody** driven
whyNot.E: Needs **no antibody** at all; her disease is driven by **antibodies to the TSH receptor**

answer: Type II hypersensitivity (IgG against a cell-surface receptor)
why: **IgG** binds the **TSH receptor** on follicular cells and **stimulates** it, causing excess hormone. Rh disease is also **IgG to a cell-surface antigen**, but there the antibody destroys cells.
chain: IgG made against the TSH receptor
IgG binds the receptor on follicular cells
Excess T3 and T4, TSH suppressed

idea.rule: Type II hypersensitivity is antibody against a cell-surface or matrix target, whether it kills, blocks or stimulates.
also: Myasthenia gravis: antibody blocks acetylcholine receptors
Goodpasture: IgG to type IV collagen
Pemphigus vulgaris: IgG to desmoglein
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia and Rh disease: IgG to red cell antigens

stem: A 24-year-old obese woman has had only 4 to 6 periods a year since menarche. She has acne and coarse dark hair on her chin and upper lip. The skin on the back of her neck is dark and velvety. Fasting insulin is raised and the LH to FSH ratio is 3 to 1. Total testosterone is mildly raised and 17-hydroxyprogesterone is normal. Her blood pressure is normal and she has no striae or easy bruising.
oneliner: 24F + obese + oligomenorrhea since menarche + hirsutism and acne + dark velvety neck skin + raised fasting insulin + LH:FSH 3:1 + mildly raised testosterone + normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone → which mechanism explains the androgen excess?
ask: Which of the following best explains her androgen excess?

options.A: Autonomous androgen release from an ovarian tumor
options.C: High insulin raising ovarian androgens and lowering SHBG
options.D: Excess cortisol stimulating adrenal androgen release
options.E: Greater aromatase activity in fat tissue lowering androgens

whyNot.A: An androgen-secreting tumor causes **rapid-onset** virilization; hers has been present **since menarche** with testosterone only **mildly raised**
whyNot.B: Would raise **17-hydroxyprogesterone**, which is **normal** here
whyNot.D: Cortisol excess would give **striae, easy bruising and hypertension**; she has **none**
whyNot.E: Aromatase turns androgens into estrogens and would **lower** androgens, yet she has **hirsutism and acne**

answer: High insulin raising ovarian androgens and lowering SHBG
why: **Obesity, acanthosis nigricans and raised fasting insulin** show insulin resistance. The high insulin acts with **LH on ovarian theca cells** to make more androgen and **lowers hepatic SHBG**, so free testosterone rises, giving hirsutism, acne and anovulation (polycystic ovary syndrome).
chain: Theca cells make more androgen (with high LH); liver makes less SHBG

idea.rule: In insulin resistance, high insulin acts as an androgen-promoting hormone in the ovary and liver.
also: Insulin sensitizers (metformin, weight loss) lower androgens and restore cycles in this disease
Acanthosis nigricans marks hyperinsulinemia in the skin
Low SHBG raises the free fraction of testosterone
Raised LH to FSH ratio favors theca-cell androgen over follicle growth

stem: In an experiment, a knockout mouse line is raised to 3 weeks of age. Compared with littermates, the knockout mice have long bones about half the normal length. Their epiphyseal growth plates are narrow with few dividing chondrocytes. Body proportions are normal. Serum growth hormone is higher than in littermates.
oneliner: Knockout mouse at 3 weeks + long bones half normal length + narrow epiphyseal plates with few dividing chondrocytes + proportionate body + high growth hormone → which factor is missing?
ask: Absence of which of the following best explains these findings?

whyNot.B: Does not explain **poor growth-plate proliferation** or a **high growth hormone**
whyNot.C: Cortisol loss does not cause **narrow plates with few dividing chondrocytes**; glucocorticoid excess, not lack, stunts growth
whyNot.D: Drives fibroblast and smooth muscle division, not the **growth-plate chondrocyte** proliferation that is lacking
whyNot.E: Thyroid hormone lack also lowers growth hormone release, whereas here **growth hormone is high**

answer: Insulin-like growth factor 1
why: **Few dividing chondrocytes, narrow plates and short, proportionate bones** show failed longitudinal growth. Growth hormone acts largely through **IGF-1** made in the liver and at the growth plate. The **high growth hormone** reflects lost negative feedback from the missing IGF-1.
chain: Liver and growth plate make IGF-1
Absent IGF-1: no feedback on pituitary, so GH rises, with short bones

idea.rule: Growth hormone makes IGF-1, and IGF-1 does the growing and feeds back on the pituitary.
also: Laron syndrome (GH receptor defect): high GH, low IGF-1, short stature
Acromegaly: high IGF-1 is the screening test
Pituitary GH deficiency: low GH and low IGF-1
IGF-1 inhibits GH release, and hypothalamic somatostatin also does

stem: A 28-year-old woman who works as a nurse has had recurrent episodes of sweating and confusion at random times of day. During an episode, plasma glucose is 38 mg/dL, serum insulin is high and C-peptide is very low. A sulfonylurea screen is negative. Symptoms resolve with intravenous glucose.
oneliner: 28F + nurse + recurrent sweating and confusion at random times + glucose 38 + high insulin + very low C-peptide + negative sulfonylurea screen + resolves with glucose → which explains the hormone pattern?
ask: Which of the following best explains this hormone pattern?

options.A: Tumor secreting proinsulin with excess C-peptide
options.B: Closure of beta-cell K-ATP channels by a drug
options.C: Antibodies that activate the insulin receptor
options.D: Insulin given by injection from outside the body
options.E: Impaired kidney clearance of circulating insulin

whyNot.A: Would raise **C-peptide** along with insulin, but hers is **very low**
whyNot.B: Would also raise **C-peptide**, and the **sulfonylurea screen is negative**
whyNot.C: Receptor activation would suppress her own insulin release, yet her **insulin is high**
whyNot.E: C-peptide is cleared mainly by the kidney, so poor renal clearance would **raise C-peptide**, not leave it **very low**

answer: Insulin given by injection from outside the body
why: The beta cell cleaves proinsulin into **insulin and C-peptide in equal amounts**. **High insulin with very low C-peptide** during hypoglycemia means the insulin did not come from her own beta cells. Injected insulin contains **no C-peptide**, and her own secretion is suppressed by the low glucose.
chain: Cleaved in granules into insulin and C-peptide
Own secretion releases both in equal amounts
Result: high insulin with low C-peptide

idea.rule: C-peptide tracks the body's own insulin output; injected insulin raises insulin alone.
also: Insulinoma: high insulin and high C-peptide
Sulfonylurea use: high insulin and high C-peptide, positive drug screen
Type 1 diabetes: low insulin and low C-peptide
In insulin-treated patients, C-peptide measures remaining beta-cell function

stem: Isolated pancreatic islets are perfused with a high glucose concentration. Glucose enters the beta cells through GLUT2, and the ATP to ADP ratio inside the cells rises. The membrane then depolarizes, and calcium enters only after the depolarization. A sulfonylurea added at low glucose reproduces the depolarization.
oneliner: Isolated islets + high glucose + GLUT2 entry + rising ATP/ADP ratio + depolarization before calcium entry + sulfonylurea mimics it → which event links ATP rise to depolarization?
ask: Which event most directly links the rise in ATP to membrane depolarization?

options.A: Inhibition of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump

whyNot.A: Pump inhibition is not shown to follow the **ATP rise**, and it is not how the **sulfonylurea** reproduces the depolarization
whyNot.C: Calcium enters only **after** the membrane has depolarized, so this follows the event
whyNot.D: Not triggered by a **rise in ATP/ADP**, and not how the sulfonylurea reproduces the effect
whyNot.E: Breaks down cyclic nucleotides; it has no link to the **ATP rise** or to depolarization

answer: Closure of ATP-sensitive K+ channels
why: Glucose is metabolized to raise **ATP**, which **closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels**. Less K+ leaves, so the membrane **depolarizes**, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and calcium triggers insulin granule release. **Sulfonylureas** close the same channel at low glucose.
chain: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and insulin is released

idea.rule: In the beta cell, glucose metabolism closes K-ATP channels, and calcium entry then triggers insulin release.
also: Sulfonylureas and meglitinides close K-ATP channels, so insulin is released regardless of glucose level
Diazoxide opens K-ATP channels and lowers insulin release
Glucokinase is the beta-cell glucose sensor
GLP-1 raises cAMP and amplifies glucose-dependent release

stem: A 12-year-old boy is far above the 99th percentile for height and has grown 12 cm in each of the last 2 years. A wrist x-ray shows open growth plates. IGF-1 is high, and growth hormone is not suppressed by an oral glucose load. MRI shows a 1.5-cm pituitary mass.
oneliner: 12M + height far above the 99th percentile + 12 cm/year growth + open growth plates on wrist x-ray + high IGF-1 + GH not suppressed by glucose + pituitary macroadenoma → which explains the growth pattern?
ask: Which of the following best explains the pattern of his growth?

options.A: Early gonadotropin release causing premature puberty
options.C: Growth hormone excess acting on unfused epiphyses
options.D: Extra X chromosome delaying plate closure
options.E: Thyroid hormone excess advancing bone age

whyNot.A: Would close growth plates **early**, but his are **open**, and it does not explain **high IGF-1 and a pituitary mass**
whyNot.B: Would not raise **IGF-1** or produce a **pituitary mass**
whyNot.D: Would not raise **IGF-1** or give **GH not suppressed by glucose** and a **pituitary mass**
whyNot.E: Would not give a **pituitary mass** or **GH not suppressed by glucose**

answer: Growth hormone excess acting on unfused epiphyses
why: A **pituitary mass with high IGF-1 and growth hormone not suppressed by glucose** is growth hormone excess. Because his **growth plates are still open**, the excess drives long-bone growth and tall stature (gigantism). After the plates fuse, the same excess enlarges hands, feet, jaw and soft tissue (acromegaly) but not height.
chain: Open growth plates respond with chondrocyte proliferation

idea.rule: The same hormone excess gives different pictures depending on whether the growth plates are open.
also: Before plate closure: gigantism with tall stature
After closure: acromegaly with enlarging hands, feet and jaw
Screening test is IGF-1; confirmation is failure of GH suppression after glucose
MRI looks for a pituitary adenoma
